subject: chemistry-1
question: In a teaching data set, breaking an O-H covalent bond inside a water molecule requires about 460 kJ/mol, while breaking a hydrogen bond between two water molecules requires about 20 kJ/mol. Which conclusion is best supported by this comparison?

options.text: Boiling water breaks its O-H covalent bonds, which is why steam is chemically different from liquid water.
Water's high boiling point reflects individual hydrogen bonds that are each only 23 kJ/mol weaker than an O-H bond.
A hydrogen bond is a weak covalent bond in which two molecules share one hydrogen atom's single electron.
The O-H bond is about 23 times stronger than the hydrogen bond, so boiling separates whole molecules without breaking O-H bonds.

explanation:
Dividing the two values gives 460 / 20 = 23, an order-of-magnitude gap between an intramolecular covalent bond and an intermolecular attraction. Vaporization supplies far less energy than 460 kJ/mol, so it overcomes only the weaker hydrogen bonds; steam is still H2O with its O-H bonds intact. Option C misdefines a hydrogen bond, which is a strong dipole-dipole attraction rather than a shared-electron bond. Option B misreads the data: the two energies differ by a factor of 23, not by 23 kJ/mol, since 460 - 20 = 440.

ELI-10: Read the numbers as a ratio, because that tells you which attraction gives way first. At 460 versus 20 kJ/mol, the covalent O-H bond is about 23 times harder to break than a hydrogen bond, so any process supplying modest energy attacks the hydrogen bonds and nothing else. Boiling is exactly that: molecules separate from one another and drift off intact, which is why steam is still water and not loose H and O atoms. Hydrogen bonds are weak individually, but a liquid holds so many of them that water still needs unusual amounts of heat to boil.
source: OpenStax — Chemistry 2e (https://openstax.org/details/books/chemistry-2e); NIST — Reference Data / Constants (https://www.nist.gov/pml)
